lead: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step path from reactants to products. Two routes from the same reactant can give two different products. The faster route has the lower activation energy and gives the kinetic product. The more stable product has the lower Gibbs free energy and is the thermodynamic product. The fastest product is not always the most stable one. Temperature decides which product dominates. Chemists use this choice when setting conditions for a synthesis, testing drug stability, or controlling a polymer process.
prereq: You need 3.1 for Gibbs free energy and 3.2 for rate laws and rate constants.

sections.h3: Mechanism, elementary steps and the rate-determining step

blocks.text: A mechanism lists the elementary steps from reactants to products. An elementary step is a single collision or bond change. Its molecularity is the number of species that take part in that step: one is unimolecular, two is bimolecular, three is termolecular and rare. Molecularity is defined only for an elementary step. The overall order comes from experiment, as in 3.2.
The rate-determining step (RDS) is the slowest step in the sequence. It controls the overall rate. If one step has a much higher barrier than the others, treat it as the RDS.
An intermediate forms and is then consumed; it does not appear in the overall equation. For a short-lived intermediate I, the steady-state approximation sets its rate of change to about zero:

blocks.where: [I] is the concentration of the intermediate I at time t; the approximation holds when I is consumed as fast as it forms.

blocks.text: This turns a mechanism into an algebraic rate law. The approximation fails if the intermediate accumulates. A mechanism is accepted only if its rate law matches measured data and it explains the products. Trapping an intermediate, by low temperature or a fast reagent, gives extra evidence.

An energy profile plots enthalpy or Gibbs free energy against reaction coordinate. The reaction coordinate is a progress variable from reactants to products. The top of the curve is the transition state, not an intermediate. Activation energy E<sub>a</sub> is the height from reactants to the transition state. It is a kinetic quantity: it sets the rate.

blocks.where: k is the rate constant; A is the pre-exponential factor; E<sub>a</sub> is the activation energy in J mol⁻¹; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is temperature in K.

blocks.text: A small E<sub>a</sub> gives a large k. A large E<sub>a</sub> gives a small k. The product energy level is a thermodynamic quantity. A lower product level means greater stability, that is, lower Gibbs free energy. Lower E<sub>a</sub> does not imply a more stable product.

The figure shows the route to B with E<sub>a</sub> = 60 kJ mol⁻¹. The route to C has E<sub>a</sub> = 90 kJ mol⁻¹. C ends 20 kJ mol⁻¹ below B. At ordinary conditions B forms faster; C is the more stable product.

Kinetic control means the product distribution is set by relative rates. The kinetic product forms faster because its route has the lower E<sub>a</sub>. Thermodynamic control means the distribution is set by equilibrium. The thermodynamic product is more stable because it has the lower Gibbs free energy. The two controls agree only by accident.

At low temperature, the factor exp(−E<sub>a</sub>/RT) changes steeply with E<sub>a</sub>, so the lower-barrier route dominates. At high temperature, both rates become large, and if the products can interconvert, equilibrium gives the more stable product.

A catalyst lowers E<sub>a</sub> by providing a new path. It speeds the reaction but does not change the equilibrium constant. A catalyst can favour a kinetic product if it lowers only that route. It cannot make a thermodynamically unfavourable product stable.

Trapping a reactive intermediate means capturing it before it reacts further. Low temperature, dilution, or a fast added reagent can do this. Trapping proves the intermediate exists and can stop a reaction at a chosen stage. In practice, temperature and catalyst are the two handles used to choose B or C.

figure.caption: Two energy profiles from the same reactant. The route to B has a 60 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier; the route to C has a 90 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier and ends 20 kJ mol⁻¹ lower.

spec.aria: Two energy profiles from the same reactant: the fast route has a 60 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier to B, the slow route has a 90 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier to C, and C ends 20 kJ mol⁻¹ lower.

examples.question: Two parallel first-order routes start from A. Route A → B has Ea(B) = 60 kJ mol⁻¹. Route A → C has Ea(C) = 90 kJ mol⁻¹. Product C is 20 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than B. The pre-exponential factors are similar. (a) Which product is favoured at low temperature? (b) Which at high temperature? (c) Name the control in each case.
steps: Compare the barriers: Ea(B) = 60 kJ mol⁻¹ and Ea(C) = 90 kJ mol⁻¹, so B has the lower barrier.
At low temperature, k = A exp(−Ea/RT). The lower Ea gives the larger k, so B forms faster and B dominates.
Compare stability: C is 20 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than B, so C is the thermodynamic product.
At high temperature, both rates are large. If B and C can interconvert, equilibrium favours the more stable product C.
Low temperature: kinetic control gives B. High temperature: thermodynamic control gives C.
examples.answer: At low temperature B is favoured by kinetic control because Ea(B) = 60 kJ mol⁻¹ is lower than Ea(C) = 90 kJ mol⁻¹; at high temperature C is favoured by thermodynamic control because C is 20 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than B.

traps: Lower Ea means faster, not more stable. A low barrier is kinetic; a low product energy is thermodynamic.
The kinetic product is not always impossible to isolate. It is less stable than the thermodynamic product, but a high barrier can stop conversion.
A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant. It changes the path and the rate.
Molecularity belongs to an elementary step. Overall order is experimental and can be zero, fractional, or negative.
The steady-state approximation is for reactive intermediates, not for reactants or final products.

quiz.a: The kinetic product is the product that forms faster because its route has the lower activation energy.
The thermodynamic product is the more stable product, with the lower Gibbs free energy.

quiz.q: Why does a lower activation energy not prove that a product is more stable?
quiz.a: Activation energy is the barrier from reactants to the transition state. Stability is set by the product energy, that is, by Gibbs free energy.

quiz.q: Two routes have Ea = 60 and 90 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K. The pre-exponential factors are equal. Estimate the ratio k_fast/k_slow.
quiz.a: k_fast/k_slow = exp[(90000 − 60000)/(8.314 × 300)] = exp(12.03) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁵. The lower-barrier route is about 1.7 × 10⁵ times faster.

quiz.q: A reaction gives B fast and C stable. Explain why B dominates at low temperature and C at high temperature.
quiz.a: At low temperature the rate ratio depends steeply on Ea, so the lower-barrier route to B wins. At high temperature both rates are large; if B and C interconvert, equilibrium favours the more stable C.

quiz.q: A catalyst lowers only the barrier to B. What happens at low temperature?
quiz.a: The route to B becomes faster still, so B is favoured more strongly under kinetic control. The equilibrium constant is unchanged.

quiz.q: Why is the steady-state approximation used for an intermediate and not for a product?
quiz.a: An intermediate is formed and consumed, so its concentration stays small and d[I]/dt ≈ 0. A product accumulates, so its rate of change is not zero.

quiz.q: What does trapping a reactive intermediate prove?
quiz.a: It proves that the intermediate exists in the mechanism, because the trapped species can be isolated or detected.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, kinetic control is used to freeze a desired intermediate or avoid a stable but unwanted by-product. Drug formulators care because a fast-forming crystal form may later convert to a more stable polymorph. Search terms: kinetic versus thermodynamic control, polymorph screening, trapping of intermediates, steady-state approximation.
